notes.body: Storage Control applies deny-by-default to the question every exfiltration attempt asks: can data move through this path? The module governs three things: storage devices (what may connect to the endpoint), file paths (where data may be written), and shares (who may read or write network storage). The device side is the most visible: USB mass storage sticks, external hard drives, phones and tablets connecting over MTP/PTP, optical media, and Bluetooth file transfer each get a policy — typically deny or read-only by default, with narrowly scoped exceptions. The path side constrains where even allowed writes may land: sensitive directories can be sealed against writes from removable sources, and application data folders can be fenced off from user-level copying. The share side extends the same logic to the network: file shares default to read-only, with read-write granted per group, per share, with justification. The unifying principle is that data movement is a privileged action, not a background capability. In the default-allow world, any process running as the user can copy any file the user can read to any device the OS recognizes — which is why the 'customer database on a USB stick' scenario is a one-line copy command. In the default-deny world, the copy hits the device policy before the first byte moves. Worked example: the Friday-afternoon insider. An employee decides to take the client list. They plug in a personal USB stick. The device class (USB mass storage) is deny-write by default for their group. The copy command fails; the attempt is logged with device ID, user, timestamp, and the file paths touched. The employee tries their phone instead — MTP storage class, same deny. They try uploading to personal cloud storage — the network egress policy (M06) denies the unapproved destination. Three paths, three denials, one alert bundle. The data never moved. Common gotcha: scoping device policy by machine instead of by user-and-machine. A 'blocked' USB stick that works when moved to another workstation is not a control; it is a suggestion. Policy must follow the device class and the user so the denial is consistent everywhere. Second gotcha: forgetting the read direction. Blocking writes stops exfiltration, but allowing reads from untrusted media invites malware in — the full policy addresses both directions, and the incident walkthrough later in this module assumes you have the logs for both.  Cover the read direction with equal seriousness. Blocking writes stops exfiltration, but unrestricted reads from untrusted media invite malware in — the stick found in the parking lot is the classic delivery vector. The complete device policy states both directions per class: the field tech's registered drive may read and write, the conference-room PC may read presentation drives but never write to them, and unknown media is denied both directions. When you write the policy table, give every class two columns — read and write — and force an explicit decision in each. Blank cells become holes.
notes.title: What Storage Control governs: devices, paths, shares

notes.body: Device policy lives or dies on its class coverage, because attackers and careless users alike route around the classes you forgot. USB mass storage is the obvious one — the classic stick — and the default posture is deny-write, with read-only or full deny as the stricter variants. But the stick is only the beginning. Phones and tablets connecting over USB present themselves as MTP or PTP storage devices: to the OS they are storage, and 'I was just charging it' is not a policy exception — if it mounts as storage, the storage policy applies. External hard drives and SSDs are USB mass storage with more capacity and the same policy. Optical media (DVD-RW) still exists in some environments and gets its own rule. Bluetooth file transfer and even some wireless presentation dongles move files without a cable — the policy must name them or they become the hole. For each class, the policy states the default (deny, read-only, or allow), the exception roles, the exception conditions, and the review date. Worked example: the 40-seat company device table. USB mass storage: default deny-write; exception: field technicians with company-registered encrypted drives. Phones/tablets (MTP/PTP): default deny — charging-only cables issued to remove the ambiguity. External HDDs: default deny; exception: IT backup role with registered drives. Optical: default deny; no exceptions (no business need found in the audit). Bluetooth file transfer: default deny; exception: none — presentation uses the approved wireless system. Five classes, five rows, zero unaddressed paths. The audit that produces this table is non-optional: you cannot write policy for device classes you have not inventoried, so the first step is always discovering what connects to your endpoints — asset management data, helpdesk tickets about 'my drive doesn't work,' and a monitor-mode observation period. Common gotcha: the 'charging' loophole. Users will insist the phone was just charging. Issue charging-only cables (no data pins) and the argument evaporates — engineering beats arguing. Second gotcha: personal vs company devices. The policy distinguishes them explicitly: company-registered encrypted drives for the exception roles, personal devices never — because you cannot verify encryption, ownership, or malware status on a personal stick, and 'just this once' is how the database leaves.  You cannot govern devices you have not discovered, so the policy project starts with an inventory. Pull from asset management, but verify: check the helpdesk ticket history for 'my drive doesn't work' and 'can't access my phone' (each ticket names a device class in use), run a monitor-mode observation period logging every storage-device connection with its class and user, and survey the departments with legitimate needs (field ops, sales, executives). The inventory will surprise you — the lab equipment with its ancient data logger, the marketing team's camera cards — and each surprise is a row in the policy table that would otherwise have been a hole.
notes.title: Device classes: the complete coverage problem

notes.body: Shares are storage too, and they get the same least-privilege treatment. The default posture for a network share is read-only for the groups that need it, with read-write granted narrowly, justified, and reviewed. Broad read-write shares are the insider's other favorite path: no USB stick required when the 'Finance' share lets every employee write — and the ransomware that encrypts mapped shares loves them too. Start with the inventory: every share, its purpose, its current permissions, and who actually uses it. Then apply the discipline: read access for the groups with a demonstrated need, write access only where the workflow requires it (the finance team writes to Finance; sales reads it), and no 'Everyone: Full Control' anywhere — that entry is a finding in every audit for a reason. Scoping follows the same per-user, per-group model as device policy: the policy engine evaluates the user and the machine, so the contractor on a loaner laptop gets different share access than the finance lead on their workstation. Worked example: the company's share redesign. Before: three shares, all 'Authenticated Users: Read/Write,' because it was easy in 2019. After: FINANCE — read for management and finance, write for finance only, reviewed quarterly. ENGINEERING — read for engineering and IT, write for engineering leads, reviewed quarterly. SHARED — read for all staff, write for department heads, with a 90-day review because shared folders accumulate sensitive data like sediment. The migration is staged: audit current usage first (who actually writes where — the logs will surprise you), announce the change, flip to the new permissions, and keep a two-week exception lane for the workflows you missed. The ransomware angle deserves emphasis: the M01 trace showed encryption spreading through mapped shares. Read-only-by-default shares do not just slow insiders; they contain the blast radius of a compromised standard user whose session can only read what the shares permit. Common gotcha: share permissions vs NTFS permissions confusion. Both layers must agree — a restrictive share with permissive NTFS (or vice versa) yields the permissive effective access. Document both, and verify effective access with a test account, not by reading the dialogs. Second gotcha: the 'temporary project share' that becomes permanent. Shares get owners and review dates like everything else in this course.  Remember that effective access is the intersection of both layers: the share permissions and the NTFS permissions must agree, or the more permissive one wins. Document both in the share record, and verify with a test account in each role — reading the dialogs is not verification. The classic failure is the 'secure' share with Everyone:Read at the share level and Users:Full at the NTFS level, or vice versa; the effective access is whatever the union permits. Your migration checklist should include an effective-access test per role per share, recorded in the ticket, before you declare the migration complete.
notes.title: Share permissions: least privilege on the network

notes.body: Legitimate business needs removable media, and the policy must serve them without becoming a hole. The carve-out pattern has four elements: company ownership, encryption, registration, and named roles. The field technician who images machines on customer sites genuinely needs a bootable USB drive — so the company issues it: a company-owned, hardware-encrypted drive, registered by serial number to the named technician, with read-write allowed by policy. If the drive is lost, the revocation procedure runs: the serial is blocked, the exposure is assessed (what data was on it — the answer should be 'nothing sensitive, by policy'), and a replacement is issued. Contrast with the hole version: 'field techs may use USB drives' — personal sticks, unencrypted, unregistered, unrevocable. The other common carve-outs follow the same pattern. The sales rep presenting at a client site: read-only access for presentations from a registered drive, time-bound to the trip, no write permission — the function needs read, so read is what is granted. The executive with the board presentation: same pattern, scoped to the event. The IT backup role: registered external drives, IT machines only, with the backup software's identity in the allowlist so only the backup process may write. Each carve-out states the role, the registered devices, the permitted direction (read, write, or both), the scope, and the review date — and each is reviewed on schedule, because roles change and drives get lost. Worked example: the lost-drive drill. A field tech reports their encrypted drive missing. Step one: block the serial in policy — the drive is now unusable on any company machine even if found. Step two: exposure assessment — pull the issuance record: what was provisioned on it? (Imaging tools and drivers; no customer data, per the provisioning standard.) Step three: document the incident, reissue, and review whether the provisioning standard held. The drill is the proof that the carve-out was engineered, not just permitted. Common gotcha: carve-out creep. 'The field techs have USB, why can't sales?' — because the exception was scoped to a role with a demonstrated need, and convenience is not a need. Every expansion request goes through the same four-element test. Second gotcha: encrypted-but-unregistered. Encryption without registration means you cannot revoke the specific device — the policy cannot name what it does not know. Registration is what makes the carve-out manageable.  Standardize what goes on the issued drives. The provisioning checklist should state exactly what is installed (imaging tools, drivers, the approved transfer utility), what is forbidden (customer data at rest — the drive is a transport, not storage), and how the drive is labeled and tracked (asset tag tied to the serial in the register). When a drive is lost, this standard is what makes the exposure assessment fast: 'per the provisioning standard, no customer data was on it' is an answer you can give confidently only if the standard exists and is followed. Audit the issued drives annually against the checklist.
notes.title: Legitimate carve-outs: encrypted, registered, named

notes.body: Every blocked storage attempt is a signal, and the incident walkthrough turns the signal into a verdict. The scenario: at 3:12 PM, the SOC receives a Detect alert — blocked USB mass-storage write on WORKSTATION-23, user j.chen, attempted files: \fileserver\finance\client_master.xlsx and two more. Step one is triage, and triage starts with context, not conclusions. Pull the alert's full context: device ID and whether the device is registered, the user's role and group, the exact file paths, the timestamp, and the user's recent alert history. Step two is pattern assessment: is this a first-time single attempt (possibly curiosity or a mistake) or part of a pattern (repeated attempts, multiple machines, off-hours)? Check the user's history for prior blocked storage, network, or execution alerts — a cluster across modules is far more significant than an isolated event. Step three is the user contact, handled as an interview, not an accusation: 'We saw a blocked write to a USB device on your machine this afternoon — can you walk me through what you were trying to do?' Innocent explanations are common: the new hire who did not know the policy, the manager trying to work from home, the misconfigured backup script. Step four is the verdict and it has three branches. Benign: document the explanation, provide the approved workflow (the secure file-transfer process), close the ticket. Policy violation without malice: document, retrain, and consider whether the workflow gap that drove the attempt needs fixing — repeated 'violations' often signal a broken legitimate process. Malicious or suspicious: escalate to incident response — isolate the machine, preserve the logs, image if warranted, and begin the insider-threat procedure per company policy. Step five is the feedback loop: whatever the verdict, the policy learns — a confusing block message gets rewritten, a missing legitimate workflow gets built, a new device class gets a rule. Worked example of the pattern that matters: j.chen's single blocked attempt turns out to be the third this week, each on a different workstation, each targeting finance files, each after 6 PM. No single alert is conclusive; the pattern across time, machines, and targets is the finding. That is why the walkthrough insists on history: the SOC triages patterns, not just events. Common gotcha: treating every block as an incident. Alert fatigue kills SOCs — the triage workflow exists to spend investigation effort proportional to the pattern's seriousness. Second gotcha: skipping the user interview. Logs tell you what happened; only the human tells you why — and 'why' is what separates the training opportunity from the insider case.
notes.title: Removable-media incident walkthrough

notes.body: Storage Control does not operate alone: it is one half of the data-protection pair, and the forensics it enables are what make the other half work. The pair is Storage Control plus Data Loss Prevention. Storage Control governs the path: may data move through this device, this share, this destination? It is identity-and-policy based — it knows who, what device, and where, but it does not inspect the content. DLP governs the content: is this data sensitive? It classifies — client lists, financial records, credentials, regulated data — and acts on the classification regardless of path. Together they cover the matrix: Storage Control stops the USB copy of anything, DLP stops the sensitive spreadsheet sent through an allowed channel. Neither alone is sufficient, and the operator should be able to explain the gap each leaves. The forensics side is where Storage Control pays for itself even when nothing is blocked. Every allowed and denied storage event is logged with the same schema: timestamp, user, machine, device class, device ID/serial, direction (read/write), file paths, byte counts, and the verdict. This log is the evidence chain for three questions investigators always ask. What left the machine? The write log with file paths and byte counts. When and by whom? The timestamp-user-machine triple. Was it authorized? The verdict field plus the exception register. Worked example: the post-incident timeline. A departing employee is suspected of taking client data. The investigator pulls the storage logs for the employee's last 30 days: USB writes (two blocked attempts, one allowed write to a registered drive — 400 MB, file paths listed), share access (read of the client folder, no anomalous volume), and cross-references the DLP log (no sensitive-content alerts on allowed channels). The timeline is built from logs, not from interviews — and the allowed write to the registered drive, with its file list, becomes the precise scope of the follow-up. Without the storage log, the investigation is guesswork; with it, it is accounting. Common gotcha: log retention shorter than the investigation horizon. Insider cases surface months later — if storage logs rotate after 30 days, the evidence is gone before the question is asked. Size retention to the threat model (a year is the common enterprise answer) and protect the log store itself. Second gotcha: collecting the logs but never reviewing the allowed events. Denied attempts get attention; allowed writes to registered devices are where the authorized-but-excessive data movement hides — sample them, especially around departures and role changes.
notes.title: Forensics, retention, and the DLP partnership

summary: Data has to leave through a path, and Storage Control closes the paths by default. This module covers device-class policy (USB, phones, external drives, optical, Bluetooth), share-permission least privilege, legitimate carve-outs with registered encrypted drives, the removable-media incident walkthrough, and the forensics and DLP partnership that make it all provable.
